One analyst, an army of agents

This is the first in a series where we share our findings and learning points from Project Toaster, an OSINT-based project (open-source intelligence: public news and social media) that used agentic AI to monitor and predict the 2026 Johor State Election (JSE). Part 1 covers what we set out to do, how we designed the experiment, and what we built. Part 2 will be the post-mortem.

01 · The OG problemHow it all started

What if one human had to cover a fast-paced, noisy election all alone, but could summon an army of agents to help?

That question started Project Toaster: two of us, an analyst and a data scientist, trying to find out whether agents could keep up with a fast-moving event that generates more news and social media than one person can read. By agents we mean small AI programs that each do one job (read an article, label a comment, judge which way a signal points) and hand their work to the next. Elections are the textbook case: a fixed deadline, a flood of posts and articles in several languages, and a scoreboard at the end that tells you whether you read the room right. In the spirit of build fast, try small and fail cheaply, the Johor State Election of 11 July 2026 was the guinea pig of choice.

It was happening soon enough
Almost two months from the day Toaster was commissioned. Long enough to build something, short enough to force choices.
We knew the theatre
We had Malaysia expertise on the team (what analysts call theatre knowledge) to design the experiment, formulate the hypotheses, and decide on sensible data metrics for the test.
It was the right shape of problem
A fast-moving, dynamic, OSINT-heavy event, as most elections are. If agents could not keep up here, the idea was not worth much.

One political fact makes everything below easier to follow. BN runs the Johor state government; PH runs the national government; the two are allies in Kuala Lumpur and rivals in this state election. In 2022 BN won Johor comfortably because turnout was low, and lowest among Chinese voters, who mostly vote against BN. Whether they show up this time is the swing everyone is watching.

Who's who, for readers new to Johor

BN
Barisan Nasional, the coalition that runs the Johor state government, led by UMNO, the Malay nationalist party. Zahid Hamidi is UMNO's president; Onn Hafiz Ghazi is the Menteri Besar (chief minister). MCA is BN's Chinese-majority party.
PH
Pakatan Harapan, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's coalition, which leads the national unity government. DAP is PH's Chinese-majority party.
PN
Perikatan Nasional, the Malay-nationalist opposition: Muhyiddin Yassin's Bersatu and Abdul Hadi Awang's PAS.
Others
Bersama, a PH splinter that stood in 15 seats; MUDA, the youth party founded by Syed Saddiq and now led by Amira Aisya, which held one seat (Puteri Wangsa) after 2022. The royals are Sultan Ibrahim of Johor, who is also Malaysia's King, and his son the Regent, Tunku Ismail. A ceramah is a political rally; the RTS Link is the rail link being built between Johor Bahru and Singapore.

Terms we use

pp
Percentage points: the difference between two percentages.
Error band
The engine's typical miss on a seat's BN vote share, about 5 pp. A seat predicted inside it is a toss-up.
In play
A seat whose predicted margin is within 10 pp; the toss-ups plus the seats that lean one way.
Dial
One of the six inputs to the prediction engine. The AI sets them; a human can override them.

02 · Project creepWhat really happened

Also known as: what happens when you give an analyst and a data scientist free rein.

What started as a little single-slice toaster build very quickly morphed into one that toasted four slices of bread at once, with a little button for those who wanted their toast just a little more toasty.

It grew into three jobs: monitor the election, predict the outcome, and push out a situation report of around 400 words. Each addition answered someone's request, from analysts who wanted the evidence to the principals who wanted a two-minute brief; the OG (original) plot, agents that monitor an election, kept having to be defended. Here is how the finished machine fits together, so that every later section has a slot.

1 · ReadNews articles, party posts, comments and royal statements come in every day.
2 · LabelCheap AI models turn each item into a structured row: what it is, who it is about, which way it leans.
3 · JudgeFive AI analysts read the aggregated rows and say which way each signal points, how strongly, and how sure they are.
4 · CalibratePlain code turns those judgments into six dials, using fixed weights.
5 · PredictA statistical engine anchored on the 2022 result recomputes all 56 seats from the dials.
6 · BriefA model writes the Daily Toast from the new numbers and the evidence that moved them.

03 · DesignThe question, the yardstick, and the hypotheses

We adopted a two-part approach. First, design the toaster: work out the problem, the hypotheses, and the indicators that would tell us whether the hypotheses were holding. Only then build the machine: find the data and build the components that track those indicators. This section is the design; sections 04 to 08 are the build.

1Design the toaster

Identify the problem
Formulate the hypotheses
Agree on appropriate indicators

2Build the machine

Obtain the necessary data sources
Build the components to track the indicators

Identifying the question

Just like all good papers, Toaster started with a list of questions and hypotheses that we wanted to test.

Placeholder · main questions

Insert the main questions the project set out to answer. The outline marks this as "insert later".

But such questions were too complex for a little machine to answer, and really belonged to big-brained human analysts with access to far more information than Toaster would ever see. We had to break them down into a question that data could answer directly.

The big questionsWhat the analysts actually want to know about Johor, its parties and its voters.
What a machine can be tested onSomething with a number attached and a scoreboard at the end.
The question we gave ToasterWhich coalition will win the JSE?

Defining what success would look like

Primary yardstick: within 5% of the result
Success would be if Toaster could predict the JSE result with a 5% margin of error. Admittedly blunt, but easy to score. (Whether the 5% is measured on seats or on each seat's vote share is settled in the Results section.)
Secondary yardstick: less to read
Toaster should help people monitor the JSE more efficiently by doing a first cut of all the data, so that humans have less raw material to monitor and mentally process.

Notice what had happened. Monitoring, the whole point of the original idea, was now the secondary yardstick; predicting the result had quietly become the main event. Oh how far we had strayed from the OG objective.

Formulating hypotheses and frameworks

We used long-existing frameworks and assumptions, building on what we knew about Johor's quirks and trying to explicitly tease out the assumptions that had become second nature. It took time. A lot of it. Even in partnership with the most expensive frontier models we could throw money at (hello, Claude Opus 4.8 Max, an AI model). Writing down what you think you know turns out to be much slower than knowing it.

Assumptions

Placeholder · assumptions

The list below is transcribed from the outline and grouped for readability. The outline marks it as work in progress, so please confirm, cut or add before publication.

The core assumption
★Whoever is able to convince voters it will meet their demands will win the most seats. The whole framework is built around this.
How the parties would play it
01BN would use the same playbook it had used for every by-election since 2022: concentrate all its resources on one campaign, focus on local issues, keep its distance from the federal government, hype how Johor has benefited from the BN state government, tap the pull of the royals, trot out Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz as the poster boy, and reduce Zahid's presence.
02Zahid was still toxic to many voters, and his presence would hurt BN's chances at the ballot box.
03Hadi's presence in Johor would indicate that PAS was making a push into the state.
04DAP's campaign would focus on federal projects like the RTS Link to try to maximise Chinese turnout.
05Bersama would split the PH vote.
06MUDA would retain Puteri Wangsa on Syed Saddiq's popularity.
07Incumbents have an advantage in their seats.
How the voters would behave
08The royals have some ability to swing the Malay vote, but we would not be able to quantify the effect.
09MCA has lost the Chinese vote. The Chinese will vote DAP if they bother to turn up.
10Low turnout benefits BN and high turnout benefits PH, because the voters who stay home in a low-turnout election are mostly Chinese, and they lean PH. This is based on the 2022 JSE, where low overall turnout, especially among Chinese voters, benefited BN.
11Where PN is not running, PN supporters will vote BN rather than PH; where it is, they will vote PN.
12The Chinese, especially those working in Singapore, are unlikely to return to vote.
What the data could tell us
13Sentiment analysis from news reporting, leader visits, likes and comments will help predict seat winners.

Framework

Our framework was a simple equation based on the core assumption: the coalition best able to meet voter demands would win. In short, voter demand + parties' ability to supply = votes. Tap any item to see which indicator it became.

Demand

What voters want, and how they are responding
+

Supply

What the parties are offering, and how well
=

Votes

Seats won, coalition by coalition

We also acknowledged that the framework would never fully cover everything that determines turnout, which depends on many factors, including the weather on the day itself.

04 · Build · the three interfacesThree interfaces for covering an election

Thinking about who would use the machine, and for what, gave us three interfaces. Each asks the AI to do something different: read, judge, or write. Monitoring is where AI extracts information. Predicting is where it makes assessments. Updating, which became the Daily Toast, is where it summarises. Keeping the three jobs separate let us decide how much to trust the AI in each. Section 09 shows the finished dashboard; sections 06 to 08 explain how each interface was built.

Interface 1

Monitoring

What it doesTracks six indicators we hypothesised would show where the election was heading (section 06 lists them).
What the AI doesExtracts information: reads posts, comments and articles and turns them into labelled, structured rows.
Interface 2

Predicting

What it doesTurns the indicators into a seat-by-seat forecast through a statistical prediction engine.
What the AI doesMakes assessments: judges which way each indicator is pointing, and how strongly, to set the engine's six dials (section 07 explains them).
Interface 3

Updating: the Daily Toast

What it doesSends a regular update with a news round-up and the latest forecast: every morning and, from 1 July, most evenings.
What the AI doesSummarises: writes about 400 words from the numbers the engine produced and the evidence that moved them.

05 · Build · what we fed itData sources, and how we weighted them

We obtained our list of candidate data sources from an extensive literature review, courtesy of Claude, and cross-referenced it against the sources we already used. The two of us then went through it together and asked two questions of every source: is it feasible to get in the time we have, and how much should it count given the question we are trying to answer? We had weeks, not months, to find data and build pipelines.

How we graded them

We sorted indicators into four broad baskets, graded A to D, on how well they have historically correlated with election results and how reliably they can be measured. The rubric grades on correlation with the eventual result: 1.0 would be perfect lockstep, 0 would be no relationship at all.

GradeRubric definitionWhat that means, and how the indicator is treated
AStrong diagnostic power, correlation at or above 0.7. Measurement validated and stable over time.Either a vote that has already happened, or opinion sampled by an instrument with a documented method. Allowed to drive the forecast on its own.
BModerate diagnostic power, correlation between 0.4 and 0.7. Some measurement concern or volatility.Sound in principle, but each has a known direction of error: approval ratings are flattered by politeness (people are kinder to pollsters than to ballots), and campaign activity is both cause and effect (parties campaign hardest where they are worried).
CWeak but real, correlation between 0.2 and 0.4. Substantial measurement or noise problems.Carries genuine information, but only after heavy processing, and never enough to overturn anything above it. Capped so it can never outweigh a higher-graded indicator.
DUnclear or negative diagnostic value in the Malaysian context.Either unavailable in practice, or so distorted that assuming nothing beats believing it. Listed with reasons, then ignored.

What we used, and why

We used the indicators below on the strength of their diagnostic ability and reliability. Official sources and polls sit at the top of the graded list; the further down the list you go, the more the measurement is something we had to construct ourselves. Two of the six live indicators, leader presence and Singapore mentions, never appeared on the graded list.

06 · Build · watchingMonitoring

We explored new types of data, and new ways of using data we already had, to get more diagnostic indicators. Six made it into the live system. What follows is the list, how each one was measured, and the thinking behind it.

IndicatorMethodologyThe thinking
Voter preference by raceOpinion poll data from reputable pollsters, found by an agent that ran a web search at every update for new polls and extracted the support levels by ethnic group.The only measured input. Everything else is a proxy.
Voter sentiment from news commentsSentiment of public comments left under mainstream media's Facebook posts on politics, labelled by target (BN, PH, PN, the Johor government, the federal government) and language (Malay, Chinese, English).Comments are where readers argue back. The caveat: we may be over-weighting a vocal minority.
Campaign activityTrack campaign activity through the parties' own social media posts about ceramahs and walkabouts.Assumes parties post about their campaign efforts on their official accounts. They did, prolifically: in the final fortnight the coalitions' pages ran from single digits a day (PH) to about 130 a day (PN).
Key leader presence in JohorTrack leaders' presence using their own social media posts: is this leader physically campaigning in Johor today?We hypothesised an inverted U: more leader activity signals a seat's importance, up to a point; beyond it, a flurry of visits signals a lack of confidence in winning.
Royal signalsThe Sultan's and Regent's social media posts, plus news articles reporting royal statements, read for explicit and coded leans.The royals are constitutionally non-partisan, so explicit endorsements are rare. Coded signals are not.
Foreign mentionsKeyword filtering of news articles and posts to capture Malaysian politicians talking about Singapore during the campaign, then a second pass to classify who said it and to whom they were appealing.Shown for context on the dashboard and in the briefing. It does not feed the forecast.
A note on the comment-sentiment indicator. Technically it is our version of social-media sentiment analysis, which we otherwise rejected (see below). The difference is scope: instead of trying to score the whole of Malaysian social media, we scored only the replies under mainstream outlets' political posts, and we read the result as relative reception among an engaged, biased sample, never as vote share.

What the monitoring views looked like

Each indicator got its own panel on the Monitoring side of the dashboard. Tap or click any image on this page to enlarge it.

Data we explored and rejected

We considered the following sources of data and rejected them for various reasons. The rejections are where knowing Malaysia mattered most.

Type of dataWhy we considered itWhy we rejected it
Prediction markets such as PolymarketHarness the wisdom of the local crowd, who might have a better sense of ground sentiment towards the parties.Hard to obtain from online sources. There was exactly one Polymarket bet on the JSE and it was thinly traded (the price barely moved).
Raw social media postsSentiment analysis of social media would be a natural way to gauge mood, with so much campaigning happening online.Hard to determine causality and direction from sentiment analysis, which remains a greenfield area and is largely limited to crude positive / neutral / negative scoring. We kept a narrower version: comments under news posts.
Chinese press sentimentOne of the few places to learn what Chinese voters are thinking.Literature and our own reading suggest Chinese-press sentiment is not diagnostic of Chinese voter sentiment. Superseded by tracking Chinese-language comments left on political news posts.
WhatsApp and Telegram closed groupsA considerable amount of news spreads through closed groups, especially among voters over 60, who tend to swing between BN and PN.No access to closed groups. We also looked at news outlets' Telegram channels to track reactions, but the Malaysian outlets we checked (Malaysiakini, Free Malaysia Today) had reactions turned off.
JAKIM's list of accredited preachers (JAKIM is the federal Islamic affairs department)An unexplored way of checking whether Johor-based preachers were endorsing candidates, as a proxy for the Malay religious vote and PAS's penetration of Johor.Hard to pin down which preachers are Johor-based even with the list, which may not be complete; many of Malaysia's religious influencers are not accredited; and tracking them down online and scraping their posts is technically expensive.
TikTok hashtagsGrowing TikTok use suggests hashtags could show which issues were gaining traction, especially among young voters.Not a data problem so much as an analytic one: we could not see how to turn hashtag traffic into a monitoring indicator with a defined direction.

Things we found but did not explore, for lack of time

YOLO v8
An image-recognition model that can count the people in a photo. Could turn small-scale ceramah turnouts into a proxy for eventual voter turnout.
Crowd-counting models
Specialised models that estimate the size of dense crowds where bodies overlap and heads are missed. Could do the same for large ceramahs.

07 · Build · predictingPredicting

AI can think through a problem and make judgments, but it struggles with complex computation unless it has tools. A model might hallucinate on a tough mental sum, yet its odds of getting the right answer are far better when you hand it a calculator. Elections can be modelled statistically, so a forecast should not be a number an LLM produces from gut feel. It should come from a model whose assumptions you can see.

Step one: build a prediction engine

To ground the prediction in a statistical model, we combined past election results with theatre knowledge about how Malaysians tend to vote, namely along racial and rural-versus-urban lines. The result is what we called the first-principles engine: first principles because it is built from an accounting identity rather than fitted to patterns. It is not machine learning. It is the arithmetic an analyst would do by hand for one seat, run consistently across all 56.

A seat's BN share = how each community votes × who actually turns out, plus the seat's own local history.The whole model in one line. Everything else is bookkeeping.

Three ideas do the work. First, communities turn out at different rates, so the electorate that actually votes is a different mix from the one on the register: in 2022 a seat that was 50% Malay on the roll was roughly 59% Malay at the ballot box, because Malay turnout was 20 points higher than Chinese turnout. Second, within each community, support for BN is roughly uniform across the state, so two numbers (Malay support, Chinese support) explain most of the variation between seats. Third, whatever those two numbers do not explain about a seat (a popular incumbent, a local grudge, the Indian vote we could not model separately) is stubbornly persistent from one election to the next, so we carry it forward.

Before we trusted it, we ran it backwards. We gave it only the statewide numbers from 2022 (Malay and Chinese support for BN, and turnout by community) together with each seat's local quirk as measured in 2018, and asked it to "predict" 2022 seat by seat. It never saw the 2022 seat results. It called 52 of 56 seats correctly and hit BN's statewide total exactly. It did the same for 2018 from 2013, an election that swung the opposite way. The panel below has the tables and the caveats, the biggest being that in live use the statewide numbers come from polls, not hindsight.

The engine exposes six dials. Set them, and it re-computes all 56 seats: the shift since 2022 in Malay support for BN and in Chinese support for BN (two dials); overall turnout and the gap between Malay and Chinese turnout (two more); and how Malays who do not vote BN split between PH and PN, in rural seats and in urban seats (the last two). On top of the dials, a seat override nudges one seat up or down when the agents have specific local evidence. After nomination day we added contest awareness, so each seat is modelled on the parties actually standing there: PN absent in 23 seats, the PH splinter Bersama in 15, two incumbents who switched coalitions.

Two benefits followed. The assumptions behind any prediction are transparent: a disagreement about the forecast becomes an argument about a specific, inspectable input. And the engine doubles as a sensitivity-analysis tool: what set of inputs would it take for BN to lose its majority? You can find out by turning the dials.

⚙️ Under the hoodThe engine, stage by stage, and how it was backtested

The model is estimated in three stages of ordinary least squares, all without intercepts, on three elections held on identical seat boundaries (2013, 2018, 2022). Every parameter is interpretable.

Stage 1, who turns out. Seat turnout is the composition-weighted average of community turnout rates. This recovers implied statewide rates for Malay (TM), Chinese (TC) and Indian (TI) voters.

Turnout_s = T_M · Malay%_s + T_C · Chinese%_s + T_I · Indian%_s + ε_s

Stage 2, effective composition. Because communities turn out at different rates, each seat's effective (voting) composition differs from its registered one.

Malay_eff_s = (Malay%_s × T_M) / Turnout_s (and similarly for Chinese, Indian)

Stage 3, how they vote. BN vote share is regressed on effective Malay and Chinese composition only. Indian voters are deliberately excluded, so their contribution, alongside candidate quality and local factors, is absorbed into the seat residual. BC should therefore be read as a Chinese-plus-Indian combined rate.

BN%_s = B_M · Malay_eff_s + B_C · Chinese_eff_s + residual_s

Stage 4, forward prediction. The previous election's residuals are carried forward at full strength as seat fixed effects; per-seat turnout is derived from composition under the chosen turnout scenario, not assumed known.

BN_pred_s = (B_M + ΔMalay) · Malay_eff_next,s + (B_C + ΔChinese) · Chinese_eff_next,s + residual_prev,s
Parameter201320182022
BM · Malay BN support84.3%65.1%60.7%
BC · Chinese (+Indian) BN support19.9%10.0%12.8%
TM · Malay turnout88.5%85.1%66.2%
TC · Chinese turnout85.6%85.4%45.8%
TI · Indian turnout93.2%88.5%36.6%
In-sample RMSE6.3 pp6.7 pp9.8 pp

Scroll sideways for the remaining columns.

RMSE is the root-mean-square error and MAE the mean absolute error, both in percentage points (pp) of BN vote share per seat. Two readings of that table matter. Malay BN support declined monotonically, 84% to 65% to 61%: BN's 2022 seat recovery (40 of 56) was not a support recovery but the product of the turnout gap and a split opposition. And the higher 2022 RMSE reflects genuinely larger idiosyncratic variance (PN competing seriously for the first time), not model deterioration.

Backtests. To predict year T from year T−1, the backtest supplies the year-T support and turnout rates as known (what polls and rolls could in principle provide) and bets only on the carried-forward residuals and the derived per-seat turnout. Two reference runs bracket each test: composition only (residuals zeroed) and an in-sample ceiling (true year-T residuals).

RunRMSEMAECorrect callsBN seats
2018 → 2022 (actual BN seats: 40)
Composition only8.86 pp7.03 pp48/5640
2018 residuals carried forward5.04 pp4.03 pp52/5640
In-sample ceiling2.77 pp1.98 pp54/5640
2013 → 2018 (actual BN seats: 19)
Composition only6.82 pp5.47 pp46/5621
2013 residuals carried forward4.71 pp3.81 pp52/5619
In-sample ceiling1.11 pp0.75 pp——

Scroll sideways for the remaining columns.

Two successful out-of-sample trials on maximally different elections, one where BN collapsed and one where it recovered, and the exact statewide BN seat count in both. The four wrong calls in 2022 (Bukit Kepong, Tangkak, Yong Peng, Parit Yaani) were all pre-flagged as marginal and offset two-for-two. Residual persistence across one cycle is strong (r = 0.74 for 2013→2018, 0.85 for 2018→2022) and decays over two (0.59), so residuals are carried forward one election only.

Known limitations, disclosed in the methodology report.

  1. The backtest is a best case: true support and turnout rates were supplied. In live use they come from polls, and input error propagates roughly one-for-one into every seat of similar composition. Real forward error will exceed 5 pp.
  2. Support levels are weakly identified; the Malay–Chinese gap is not. Effective Malay and Chinese shares are near-complementary (r ≈ −0.95), so the data pins down the gap (~48 pp in 2022) far more tightly than the individual levels. Translating a poll number directly onto BM is less exact than the dials imply.
  3. Indian voters are not separately modelled.
  4. The opposition side is modelled coarsely: the engine is validated for BN performance, and PH-versus-PN outcomes rest on weaker footing.
  5. One state, two transitions, 56 seats. Parameters do not transfer elsewhere without refitting, and a boundary redelineation would break residual carry-forward.
  6. Residuals are a one-cycle asset; the baseline should always be the most recent election.

Defensible as a scenario tool and a device for spotting marginal seats. Not defensible as a point predictor of individual marginals, a poll-free forecast, or a PH-versus-PN model.

Step two: put AI agents in charge of the dials

With the engine in place, the AI had a narrow job: turn the monitoring indicators into the engine's six inputs. Five specialist agents each read one slice of the evidence, and a sixth component, a rules-based editor (the dashboard calls it the Synthesising Agent), combines their views into the six numbers and the seat overrides. We called the five the analysts.

Voter-preference poll arithmetic
An agent runs a web search at every update for new opinion polls and extracts support levels by ethnic group. The shifts in Malay and Chinese BN support are then plain subtraction from the 2022 baselines. The only measured input, so it dominates when a fresh, relevant poll exists.
Voter-response judgment
Reads the comment-sentiment index and party-page engagement, and keeps the two apart. What commenters say (warm or hostile) may move the support dials; how many of them show up (likes, shares, comments) may only move the turnout dials. Loud is not the same as persuaded. Owns four of the six numbers.
Campaign judgment
Reads per-seat campaign intensity against each seat's 2022 baseline. Activity shows a party is active in a seat, not that it is winning it; the hard call is whether heavy activity is persuasion or defence. Sole owner of the seat overrides.
Leader-interest judgment
Its AI judges one thing: where the non-BN Malay vote is splitting between PH and PN, rural and urban separately, from where party leaders physically go in Johor. The same presence data also feeds three other dials by formula (a Zahid drag on Malay support, a mobilisation lift on turnout, and the turnout gap), which is why the weight table below shows it on five rows.
Royal-signals drift formula
No judgment call here: a fixed formula adds up the royal items already read in the extraction step, for which side they favour and how loudly. It can nudge only the Malay support dial.
The editor no AI
Combines everyone's signals into the final six dials, the seat overrides, an overall confidence and the executive summary shown on the dashboard.

The voter-preference agent's condition was never met. No Johor poll was published during the campaign, so in all 74 updates the poll had no say, and the two support dials were set entirely by the other analysts' judgments, which the system calls drift: movement proposed without a poll behind it.

Code computes; the AI only classifies and judges direction.The rule that made every number on the dashboard traceable.

The AI does no arithmetic. It may copy a number out of a poll; it never computes one. What an analyst hands on is three judgments: a direction (BN stronger or weaker), a size band (small, moderate, large) and a confidence band (low, medium, high), with reasoning and citations attached. An analyst with nothing reliable to say abstains, and a silent analyst never dilutes the others. Ordinary code then turns the bands into numbers using fixed, published weights, so the same evidence always moves the dials by the same amount.

The pipeline, end to end

Every number on the dashboard is built by a chain of small, inspectable steps. Some are an AI model reading text; some are plain arithmetic. The three-card legend is the plain version; the diagram under it is for the technical reader, with the system's own component names and a plain-English tag on each. Tap any node to see what it does, and which nodes it reads from and writes to.

🤖 Extraction
An AI model reads unstructured text and labels it, turning posts, comments and articles into clean structured rows. It reads; it does not weigh the race.
🧠 Judgment
An AI model reasons over already-aggregated data and emits an analytical signal: a direction, a strength and a confidence, with its reasoning and citations.
⚙️ Deterministic
Plain code, no AI. Counts, formulas and weighting. This is where labels become an index and a signal becomes a number on the dial.

On a small screen the seven stages run top to bottom.

Over the campaign the extraction models processed thousands of items a day. For scale: the final week alone held about 2,400 news items and 2,800 party posts in the feeds, and by polling day the sentiment index rested on roughly 114,000 labelled comments in its trailing two-week window. The judgment agents, by contrast, ran on a twice-daily schedule once the pipeline was stable (the June count also includes re-runs while we were still building it), and they never saw a raw comment. They saw the index.

⚙️ Under the hoodWho moves each dial, by how much, and the poll blend

Only certain analysts own each dial, each with a fixed weight. Owners combine as a weighted average, never a sum, so agreement reinforces direction but can never exceed the strongest single owner. The band step is how far a small, moderate or large signal moves the dial, before the confidence factor trims it by ×0.33, ×0.66 or ×1.00.

The two support deltas are the only polled dials, so they blend a measured poll with the analysts' drift. A fresh, Johor-specific poll dominates; the drift (capped at ±8 pp) only fills in when polling is stale or absent, which in this campaign was always.

final_Δ = poll_confidence × poll + (1 − poll_confidence) × drift

Models in the shipped pipeline (from the call logs): GPT-5.5 for the judgment agents, the news extractor, the royal-feed reader, the poll search (with web search) and the briefing writer; GPT-4.1 for classifying party posts; GPT-4o for labelling comments; GPT-4o-mini for the cheap gates (is this post about politics? does this article mention Singapore politically?). Cheap models for high-volume yes/no work, the expensive one for judgment.

08 · Build · briefingUpdating: the Daily Toast

The third interface is the easiest to explain. After the morning update, and from 1 July the evening one too, a model wrote a short situation report and pushed it to the principals on Telegram. It was given two things: a digest of how the forecast had moved since the last update, with every number marked authoritative and never to be recomputed, and the new ground evidence the agents had read. Its instructions were to synthesise rather than enumerate, lead with the bottom line, and make the causal link explicit: the new evidence is why the forecast moved.

Here is a real one, from the evening of 7 July, the day the forecast dropped five seats in a single cycle. It was written for people already following the race, so it is dense with names (Najib Razak is the jailed former prime minister whose pardon became a campaign issue; the others are ministers and party elders); if you read one paragraph, read "What moved today". The mood scores it quotes run from −1 to +1, and its "error band (5%)" is the engine's typical seat-level miss.

🍞 Daily Toast · 7 July, evening

1. State of play

The model projected BN winning 38 of 56 seats — but 3 of those are inside the error band (5%), and a further 7 are won by under 10%. That still puts BN clearly above the 29-seat majority line, but the race is less locked than the headline seat count suggests because the opposition now has 11 narrow holds within 10 points of BN's reach, up from 6 this morning. Serom and Kota Iskandar are the tightest projected BN wins, so they should be treated as true toss-ups rather than leans. The broader campaign mood is mixed for BN: Malay comments toward BN warmed from 0.003 to 0.063 over the last five days, and mood toward the Johor government improved more sharply from −0.045 to 0.222. PH's Malay comment mood deteriorated from 0.175 to −0.029, which helps explain why BN still has a majority path despite today's seat losses. The Najib pardon issue is now a central risk because Nazifuddin Najib linked a big BN win in Kluang to support for Najib's release, and Anwar used Serom to frame the election as a vehicle for freeing Najib. BN leaders Hishammuddin Hussein and Azalina Othman Said are trying to separate the election from the pardon process. Opposition fragmentation still helps BN because PN is absent in 29 seats and Bersama is contesting 15, but PH's ground push is now reducing that advantage in several urban and marginal BN seats.

2. What moved today

BN's projection fell from 43 seats this morning to 38 seats tonight, still above the 29-seat majority line but with a materially thinner cushion. The main model driver was Malay support for BN being cut from 3.1 points above its 2022 level to only 0.53 points above 2022, which overwhelmed the unchanged Chinese BN support reading of −1.32 points versus 2022. Turnout did not drive the move because the target stayed at 56 and the Malay–Chinese turnout gap stayed at 20. Rural non-BN Malay alignment moved from 3 points toward PN versus 2022 to 2 points toward PN, which slightly helped PH where both opposition parties are actually on the ballot. The seat evidence was sharper than the statewide parameters: Tangkak, Layang-Layang, Endau, Tenggaroh and Tiram flipped from BN to the opposition column. Serom, Johor Jaya and Kota Iskandar slipped into BN toss-up territory. Rengit and Larkin are now only narrowly ahead for BN.

3. Singapore mentions

Anwar repeatedly drew a boundary around Singapore's role, saying Malaysia should not ask another country to interfere in its elections, even though companies in Singapore could be informed to ease voting arrangements for Malaysian workers. He also said Sunday voting would better suit Malaysians working half-days in Singapore, but stressed the Election Commission is independent. On the JS-SEZ, Anwar rejected claims that Johor alone controls the project, and Tengku Zafrul framed Singapore cooperation as a federal delivery story. Lim Kit Siang used Singapore to discuss overseas Malaysians and return migration.

Tue 7 Jul 2026 · 18:00 Singapore time · 496 words

Model output from the logs, verbatim apart from typography; the header line was added. The numbers it quotes came from the engine; the model was not allowed to compute any of them. One error rode along into the campaign's last day: the briefing's instructions carried a wrong count, 29 seats without a PN candidate, where the engine's own line-up data (and section 07) say 23. The 29 is a coincidence with the 29-seat majority line. We come back to this in the post-mortem.

09 · The machineWhat the final product looked like

34
days of live operation, 8 June to polling day
74
AI update cycles, each re-reading the evidence and re-setting the dials
25
dashboard versions shipped while it was running
56
seats re-forecast on every cycle

The dashboard had two faces. Monitoring showed the evidence, indicator by indicator, plus raw news and social feeds for anyone who wanted to read the source. Prediction showed the forecast: the seat count against the majority line, which seats were in play, the seat-by-seat table, and the AI reasoning panel explaining why the dials sat where they did. Tucked behind a blue tab on the left edge of the Prediction view was the third thing: the manual override sidebar, the one place where a person could take the controls.

Opening it laid out every parameter the engine runs on as a slider, with the AI's current setting on each and a small “AI” badge saying who had set it. An analyst could drag any of the six dials, add or remove a seat override, or, after nomination day, adjust three contest settings the agents did not set: how much of the PH vote the Bersama splinter takes where both stand, where the vote of an absent PN goes, and whether to trim a seat's local lean when its sitting member was not standing again. All 56 seats re-computed as the slider moved. Two buttons pinned at the top kept the what-ifs honest: one restored the AI's assessed parameters, the other set every dial to the 2022 baseline, which showed what the structural model alone would predict before any judgment was applied.

How the forecast moved over the campaign

Because every cycle was archived, we can replay the forecast. Drag the slider, or hover the chart, to see the seat count and the six dials as they stood at any update. The dashed line is the 29-seat majority; the marker on 1 July is nomination day, when the engine switched to modelling each seat's actual line-up.

—

Every AI cycle: the seat count, the six dials, seat overrides and confidence. Lean dials are shifts from the 2022 split, positive towards PH. Scroll sideways on a small screen.

Seat counts are what the dashboard displayed at the time, including the seat overrides. The two lean dials show how the non-BN Malay vote is assumed to split between PH and PN, as a shift in percentage points from the 2022 split (rural 26% to PH, urban 49%); positive means more PH-leaning. Several cycles can land on one day, which is why the line sometimes flickers. Before 1 July every seat was modelled as a three-way contest; from 1 July the engine used the real candidate list.

10 · Scoring the toastResults

The forecast was frozen at the 18:00 close of polls on 11 July at BN 38 of 56, with 20 seats flagged as in play and five of BN's projected wins inside the engine's own error band. The yardstick we set ourselves was a 5% margin of error.

Three threads Part 1 leaves hanging

  • The poll term never fired. With no Johor poll all campaign, the two support dials ran entirely on the analysts' judgment. How much did that cost?
  • The briefing carried a wrong count of seats without a PN candidate (29, not 23) from start to finish. Did it matter?
  • BN 38 with 20 seats in play. How close was that, seat by seat, and were the seats we flagged the ones that moved?
